Presented by Group 14A:
OSTEOPOROSIS
Jarrin Ahmed, Abygaile Alexis, Daniella Arabova, Marilin Contreras, 
Monnel Garraway, Gabriella Morales, Elizabeth Teper,  David Wang

• Chronic, progressive bone disease that 
causes bones to become more brittle, weak, 
and more likely to fracture. 
• Occurs when the body breaks down bone 
tissue faster than it can replace it. 
• Leads to deterioration of the bone’s internal 
structure. 
• Early detection, proper nutrition, medication 
adherence, fall prevention, and weight-
bearing and resistance exercises are essential 
to slowing down bone loss and reducing the 
risk of fractures. 
WHAT IS 
OSTEOPOROSIS?
Normal Bone Osteoporosis

Non-Modifiable Risk Factors:
• Age
• Gender (Postmenopausal females)
• Family history/genetics
• Ethnicity (Caucasian and asian individuals)
CAUSES & RISK FACTORS
01
Modifiable Risk Factors:
• Nutritional deficiencies (low calcium and 
vitamin D)
• Physical Inactivity (sedentary lifestyle)
• Substance Use (smoking, alcohol consumption) 
• Eating Disorders (anorexia, severe malnutrition) 
02
03
Medication Induced:
• Glucocorticoids: Long term oral therapy (e.g 
prednisone) is a leading cause of secondary 
osteoporosis by decreasing bone formation & 
increasing bone resorption
• Anticonvulsants: Certain seizure medications 
can increase Vitamin D metabolism & reduce 
calcium absorption 
• Hormone Blockers: Aromatase inhibitors used 
in breast cancer treatment and androgen 
deprivation therapy used in prostate cancer 
lower sex hormone levels, accelerating bone 
loss
04
Medical Conditions:
• Endocrine disorders: Hyperparathyroidism, 
Hyperthyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, Type 1 or 
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
• Gastrointestinal Disorders: Celiac disease, IBD, 
Bariatric surgery

Prevention
• Educate patients on concurrent 
medical conditions and 
medications that increase the 
risk of losing bone mass
• Encourage safe mobility
• Implement home safety 
measures that prevent falls 
(handrails, non-slip mats for the 
bathtub, handrails, reducing 
clutter, etc.)
• Highlight the importance of 
preventing fractures
Health Promotion
• Ensure you are receiving the 
daily recommended dose of 
Vitamin D (400 to 1,000 IU) and 
Calcium (1,000-1,300 mg)
• Participate in:
⚬ Weight-bearing activities 
daily
⚬ Exercises that improve 
balance (to reduce fall risk)
• Avoid the consumption of 
alcohol and smoking 
(increases the risk of bone 
loss)
Early Detection
• DEXA or DXA screening:
⚬ Women who are >65 years 
old
⚬ Women who are 
postmenopausal <65 
years old with at least one 
risk factor.
• Monitoring FRAX (fracture risk 
assessment tool) scores 
• Warning signs such as an 
unexplained loss of height
• Risk assessments that include 
fracture history 
PREVENTION/HEALTH PROMOTION/ 
EARLY DETECTION

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
Often asymptomatic in the early stages: Bone density 
gradually decreases without noticeable pain or physical 
discomfort as bone density gradually decreases. 
Fractures: As bones become weaker, the risk of fractures 
increases.
• Common sites: 
⚬ Spine (vertebrae)
⚬ Hips
⚬ Wrists
Back pain and muscle spasms
Kyphosis and height loss: Compression fractures in the 
spine can cause a hunched posture and a gradual loss 
of height.
Other effects: Changes in posture and body shape may 
affect body image, and spinal changes can sometimes 
contribute to constipation.
Osteoporosis is undetectable on routine X-rays 
until there has been significant demineralization.

GOLD STANDARD: DEXA or DXA Scan
Low-dose-radiation x-rays are used to determine the bone mineral density (BMD) of the 
hip, wrist, or spine; the T-score result is compared to standard values for a 
demographically similar individual to determine the presence and severity of 
osteoporosis.
Nursing Responsibilities
• Pre-Procedure:
⚬  Screening Assessment: Identify high-risk clients: women 65 years old or over, 
men 70 years old or older, postmenopausal women with risk factors
⚬ Patient Education
￭ Explain the DEXA scan procedure to the client
￭ Instruct the client to hold any calcium supplements for at least 24 hours 
before the DEXA scan if the physician orders; because local calcium 
concentrations can screw results
￭ Inform the client to remove any metal objects around the pelvic and spinal 
regions that can interfere with x-ray results
• Intra-Procedure:
⚬ Position the client supine and implement fall and fracture precautions. 
• Post-Procedure:
⚬ Review T-score and notify provider if it indicates osteoporosis
⚬ Implement fall-risk precautions; Assist with ADLs as needed 
⚬ Patient Education 
DIAGNOSIS

• Standard X-rays: Used for the later stages of 
osteoporosis, to monitor disease progression
⚬ E.g identifying new fractures or height loss.
• Lab & Blood Tests: No lab values are specific to 
confirming osteoporosis.  However, testing 
Vitamin D, Calcium, Albumin, and Phosphate 
levels can rule out other medical conditions.
OTHER DIAGNOSTIC TESTS

• Alendronate (Fosamax)
⚬ Slows bone breakdown 
preventing fractures
• Denosumab(Prolia)
⚬ Decreases bone resorption 
and preserves bone 
density 
• Teriparatide (Forteo)
⚬ Stimulates new bone 
formation
MEDICATION ADHERENCE IS KEY 
FOR   LONG TERM OSTEOPOROSIS 
MANAGEMENT
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
Calcium Intake and 
Vitamin D 
 Fracture Prevention Medications
• Calcium helps build and 
maintain strong bones
⚬ If calcium intake is 
too low, the body can 
pull calcium from 
bones making them 
weaker
• Vitamin D helps absorb 
calcium from intestines
Together both help maintain bone 
density and reduce bone loss
• Preventing fractures by 
reducing fall risk
⚬ Examples:
⚬ Removing rugs and 
clutter
⚬ Wearing supportive non-
slip shoes
⚬ Poor lighting
• Encouraging safe weight 
bearing exercises to 
maintain bone strength.
⚬ Examples:
⚬ Walking
⚬ Stair climbing
⚬ Low impact aerobics

MEDICATION MANAGMENT & NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES 
Bisphosphonates (Alendronate, 
Risedronate, Ibandronate, 
Zoledronic Acid)
Receptor Activator of Nuclear 
Factor Kappa-B Ligand (RANKL) 
Inhibitor (Denosumab)
Parathyroid Hormone 
Analogue (Teriparatide)
Calcium & Vitamin D 
Supplementation
Inhibits osteoclast-mediated 
bone resorption to decrease 
bone loss, they are taken by 
mouth daily or weekly
Monoclonal antibody that 
blocks RANKL/osteoclast 
activity which reduces bone 
resorption and is given 
subcutaneously every 6 
months
Anabolic agent that stimulates 
new bone formation and 
increases bone strength and 
mineral density, it is self-
administered subcutaneously 
each day and must be 
refrigerated.
May be prescribed alongside 
osteoporosis medications. If 
calcium supplements are 
needed, divide the daily 
amount because the body 
absorbs calcium poorly in 
doses greater than 500 mg at 
one time.Nursing 
Responsibilites:• Assess bone-health risks: Ask about previous fractures, calcium intake, exercise, 
corticosteroid use, smoking, alcohol, and caffeine.
• Review medication safety: For bisphosphonate therapy, check for a history of Barrett 
esophagus, low serum calcium, or pregnancy, which the textbook lists as contraindications.
• Teach oral bisphosphonate administration: Take in the morning on an empty stomach with 
250 mL of water; remain sitting or standing upright for at least 30 minutes. Don’t take calcium 
supplements at the same time.
• Monitor and report adverse effects: Bisphosphonates can cause GI symptoms and, rarely, 
ulcers, osteonecrosis of the jaw, or atypical femur fractures. Denosumab can cause 
hypocalcemia, cellulitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw, or atypical femur fractures.
• Reinforce adherence and follow-up: Explain the purpose of the prescribed therapy and 
calcium/vitamin D support. If denosumab is stopped, another medication may be started to 
reduce rapid bone-density loss.

PATIENT & FAMILY EDUCATION
• The patient and family should be educated on 
adequate intake of both calcium and vitamin D, as 
they help maintain bone strength. 
• Educate on the importance of participating in weight-
bearing and muscle-strengthening exercises. 
• Encourage the cessation of smoking, limiting alcohol, 
and taking prescribed medications as directed. 
• Educate on fall-prevention measures, such as 
removing hazards in the household and using 
assistive devices.
• Encourage the patient to attend regular follow-up 
appointments and to report any new or sudden back 
pain, height loss, or suspected fractures as soon as 
possible.

DISCHARGE PLANNING 
AND HOMECARE
• Evaluate the patient’s living environment for fall hazards, including poor 
lighting, loose rugs, stairs, and lack of bathroom safety equipment. 
• Assess the patient’s mobility, ability to perform ADLs, balance, and the 
need for assistance before discharge. 
• Collaborate with occupational and physical therapy to improve mobility, 
assess needed assistive device, and determine whether home health 
services as necessary. 
• Review prescribed medications before discharge, assess medications, 
identify potential interactions. 
• Arrange follow-up care with the primary care provider or specialist to 
monitor osteoporosis progression, fracture risk, and treatment 
effectiveness. 
• Coordinate access to home health nursing, rehabilitation services, 
transportation assistance, or community support programs for patients 
with limited independence.

A nurse is assessing four clients during a routine health screening. 
The nurse understands that certain medical conditions, medications, 
and lifestyle factors can increase the risk of developing osteoporosis. 
Which client is at the greatest risk for developing osteoporosis?
A. A 45-year-old male who exercises regularly, eats a balanced diet, 
and has a family history of hypertension.
B. A 68-year-old postmenopausal female who has been taking 
prednisone daily for rheumatoid arthritis for the past 5 years.
C. A 60-year-old female who walks daily, consumes calcium-rich 
foods, and takes vitamin D supplements.
D. A 52-year-old male who has a sedentary lifestyle but maintains 
adequate calcium and vitamin D intake.
NCLEX STYLE QUESTION #1

• B — Correct:  This client has several significant risk factors for osteoporosis. 
Following menopause, estrogen levels decrease, which accelerates bone loss. 
Long-term prednisone use further increases the risk by decreasing bone 
formation, increasing bone breakdown, and reducing calcium absorption. 
Rheumatoid arthritis also contributes to bone loss through chronic inflammation 
and reduced mobility. The combination of these factors places this client at the 
greatest risk.
• A — Incorrect:  Although osteoporosis can affect men, this client has fewer 
major risk factors. Regular exercise and a balanced diet help maintain bone 
strength. A family history of hypertension is not a recognized risk factor for 
osteoporosis.
• C — Incorrect:  Although age and menopause increase osteoporosis risk, this 
client practices several protective behaviors. Walking provides weight-bearing 
activity that helps maintain bone strength, while adequate calcium and 
vitamin D support bone health. These habits do not eliminate the risk but help 
reduce it.
• D — Incorrect:  A sedentary lifestyle is a risk factor because physical inactivity 
contributes to decreased bone strength. However, this client has fewer 
significant risk factors compared with the older postmenopausal female taking 
long-term corticosteroids. Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake also support 
bone health.
ANSWER & RATIONLES

A 78-year-old female client with a history of osteoporosis is brought to the emergency department after falling 
while getting out of bed. She reports severe right hip pain and is unable to stand or bear weight on her right leg.
Blood pressure 148/86 mmHg
Heart rate 108 beats/min
Respiratory rate 22 breaths/min
SpO  96% on room air₂
Pain 9/10, right hip
Physical assessment: Right leg shortened and externally rotated, with significant pain on movement
Medical history: Osteoporosis, hypertension, previous vertebral compression fracture
NCLEX STYLE QUESTION #2
During the nursing assessment, the following findings are documented:
Complete the following sentence using the drop-down options.
The nurse should recognize that the client is most likely experiencing (1) ______ and should prioritize (2) ______.
Drop-down 1:
A. Osteoarthritis of the right hip
B. Right hip fracture 
C. Acute lumbar radiculopathy
D. Right hip muscle strain
Drop-down 2:
A. Assist the client to ambulate to assess mobility 
B. Apply a heating pad to the affected hip
C. Immobilize the affected extremity and assess 
neurovascular status
D. Perform passive range-of-motion exercises

• B — Right hip fracture (Correct): Older adults with osteoporosis have 
decreased bone density, making them more susceptible to fragility 
fractures following minor trauma. Severe hip pain, inability to bear weight, 
and a shortened, externally rotated leg are classic findings associated with 
a displaced hip fracture. Imaging is required to confirm the diagnosis.
• A — Osteoarthritis (Incorrect): Osteoarthritis typically causes gradual joint pain, 
stiffness, and decreased range of motion. It does not usually cause sudden severe 
pain, limb shortening, or external rotation immediately following a fall.
• C — Acute lumbar radiculopathy (Incorrect):  Lumbar radiculopathy occurs when 
a spinal nerve root becomes compressed, often causing radiating pain, 
numbness, or tingling down the leg. It does not explain the client's visible limb 
deformity.
• D — Right hip muscle strain (Incorrect):  Muscle strains can cause pain and 
limited mobility but do not typically produce limb shortening or external rotation. 
The client's age, osteoporosis history, and assessment findings strongly suggest a 
fracture rather than a soft tissue injury.
Drop Down 1

• C — Immobilize and assess neurovascular status (Correct):  The nurse should 
maintain the affected extremity in its current supported position, avoid 
unnecessary movement, and assess circulation, sensation, movement, skin 
temperature, and distal pulses. These assessments help identify possible 
neurovascular compromise. The nurse should also notify the provider, monitor 
vital signs, administer prescribed pain medication, and prepare the client for 
diagnostic imaging and possible surgical management.
• A — Assist with ambulation (Incorrect):  Attempting to ambulate a client with a 
suspected hip fracture could worsen the injury, increase pain, and cause further 
displacement of the fractured bone. The client should remain on bed rest until 
evaluated and stabilized.
• B — Apply heat (Incorrect):  Heat does not stabilize a fracture and may worsen 
swelling during the acute injury period. The nurse should focus on preventing 
movement and further injury rather than applying heat.
• D — Perform passive range-of-motion exercises (Incorrect):  Moving the affected 
hip could worsen fracture displacement, damage surrounding tissues, and 
increase pain. Range-of-motion exercises are inappropriate until the fracture has 
been evaluated and the healthcare team determines when movement is safe.
Drop Down 2
